To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the clearance of virus from lymphoid tissue is the fastest process determining the time course of HIV-1 viremia, that the clearance of HIV-1 from the blood is about 20 day− 1, and that the clearance of HCV from the blood is approximately 2.5 day− 1.

the fast clearance of HIV-1 during therapy probably reflects virus clearance from lymphoid tissue, that plasma apheresis is a good measure for the plasma clearance rate, that current estimates are consistent with a plasma virus clearance rate of approximately 20 day-1 and a death rate of virus producing cells of 0.5-1 day-1, that the virus production rate is approximately 1 billion virions/day for HIV-1 and 10 billion for HCV, and that extending current models
the clearance of LT HIV-1 is fast, that the clearance of HCV is slow, and that the production of HCV is fast.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the large LT pool of HIV-1 and HCV on the kinetics in the plasma.
the effects of virus release from the LT compartment on estimates for kinetic parameters in HIV-1 and HCV infection.
the effects of virus localization on the interpretation of experimental data and the estimates for viral kinetic parameters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the kinetic parameters of HIV-1 and HCV are not yet fully resolved, although the extended models provide a good framework for future studies.
current models for HIV-1 and HCV are insufficiently detailed to make reliable predictions for treatment efficacy.
the kinetic parameters of HIV-1 and HCV infections can be estimated only after the virus production and clearance processes in both the blood and the LT compartments have been quantified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LT compartment has to be considered for HIV-1, but not necessarily for HCV.

, for both HIV-1 and HCV, the LT compartment is important in determining the kinetics in plasma, and that estimates for kinetic parameters are sensitive to the assumptions made about virus clearance from LT.
the LT compartment is not only important for the immune response but also has a large effect on virus kinetics in the blood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the release of LT virus is a crucial component for the understanding of the dynamics of chronic HIV-1 and HCV infections and that it needs to be included in the modeling of these infections.
the release of virus from LT affects HIV-1 and HCV plasma virus kinetics.
the kinetics of HIV-1 and HCV in the blood compartment can be understood only by considering the virus pool in the LT compartment.
